# Weekly Book Topics 50Q - week of 30 Aug 2026 (Sun 30 Aug - Sat 5 Sep)

*Auto-generated for UPSC CSE 2027 prep. Feeds the website's Sectional practice flow. Static book-topic set, not current affairs.*

## Week focus

**Basis:** the **Sunday Sweep dated 2026-08-30**, which plans **Sun 30 Aug -> Sat 5 Sep 2026** - the upcoming Monday-to-Sunday block after this Sunday run, sitting in the **second half of F7** and straddling the Phase 1A / Phase 1B boundary (Phase 1B opens Tue 1 Sep). The Sweep's Sunday row asks explicitly for the Book-topics 50Q to be run "against Laxmikanth Ch 30 (High Court) the same evening while Art 226/227 is warm", so the set is weighted to that anchor and then covers the rest of the week's static reading in proportion to the hours the Sweep allots it.

**No repeats.** The last six book-topics sets (26 Jul, 02 Aug x2, 09 Aug x2, 11 Aug, 16 Aug, 23 Aug) closed Polity through the Supreme Court and PIL (Laxmikanth Ch 14-29), Vivek Singh through Ch 11 (agriculture), Spectrum through Ch 25 (Partition) and the constitutional-developments thematic, physical and human geography (NCERT-11 complete, NCERT-12 Ch 1-3), Shankar Ch 5-6, space and defence technology, and India-US / India-China. **Nothing in this week's set repeats any of them.** The judiciary appeared last week only as the Supreme Court (Ch 26-29); this week is the High Court and below, which is new chapter ground and is deliberately written around the *contrast* with last week's material rather than restating it. Ancient History has never appeared in a book-topics set before - this is its first.

**Verification note.** Three items were web-checked before use: the **March 2022 MoEFCC exemption of SDN-1 and SDN-2 genome-edited plants** from Rules 7-11 of the 1989 Rules (Q48), the **BioE3 Policy** name and 2024 Cabinet approval (used in the checklist only), and the **Sixteenth Finance Commission award period 2026-27 to 2030-31** (Q19 explanation). Nothing here is claimed to be a verbatim UPSC PYQ; the stems follow UPSC's statement-based, pair-matching, chronology and single-best-answer patterns, but all fifty are newly written.

## How to use

One sitting, **60 minutes, timed, no notes**. Mark and move; do not linger on a statement you cannot place.

Then debrief only two categories: **wrong answers** and **lucky guesses**. For each, write one line saying *why the wrong statement is wrong* - not which option was right. In this set the traps are almost all of one kind: a provision that exists for one institution being attributed to a neighbouring one (distinguished jurist, SC only; retirement age 62 vs 65 vs 62-for-State-PSC; GEAC under MoEFCC not DBT; PMKSY under MoFPI but FSSAI under Health). That is exactly the confusion a single comparative table fixes and no amount of re-reading does.

**Benchmark:** the Easy set (15 Q) should be near-perfect. More than three dropped there means the chapter has not set, and the fix is to re-read it the same evening, not to do more questions. Difficulty mix is **15 Easy / 25 Moderate / 10 Hard**. Come back for a blind re-take on Wednesday, and again the following Sunday before the F7 close-out.

## Answer key with explanations

**Q1. Answer: (a)** - *Easy* - Art 214 - a High Court for each State; Art 215 - every High Court is a court of record with power to punish for contempt. Art 216 leaves the strength of a High Court to be determined by the President/Parliament - no maximum is prescribed by the Constitution, unlike the Supreme Court where Parliament fixes the number by law. Hence statement 2 is wrong.

**Q2. Answer: (b)** - *Moderate* - Art 217 gives only two routes to a High Court judgeship: ten years in judicial office in India, or ten years as an advocate of a High Court (or of two or more such courts in succession). The 'distinguished jurist' route exists only for the Supreme Court under Art 124(3)(c). This asymmetry is a standing Prelims trap.

**Q3. Answer: (b)** - *Easy* - A High Court judge holds office until the age of 62 (raised from 60 by the 15th Amendment Act, 1963). A Supreme Court judge retires at 65. Any question of age is decided by the President after consultation with the Chief Justice of India, and that decision is final.

**Q4. Answer: (d)** - *Hard* - Art 226 is wider - it lies for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights 'and for any other purpose', i.e. for ordinary legal rights too. But it is a constitutional right, not itself a Fundamental Right, and its exercise is discretionary - so a High Court may refuse relief, whereas the Supreme Court cannot refuse under Art 32. The 15th Amendment (1963) extended Art 226 to authorities outside a High Court's territory where the cause of action arises wholly or partly within it. Statement 2 is therefore wrong.

**Q5. Answer: (b)** - *Moderate* - Art 227 covers all courts and tribunals in the State except military courts/tribunals, and is both judicial (revisional) and administrative (calling for returns, framing rules, prescribing forms, settling fees). It is broader than Art 226 in one respect - it can be exercised suo motu, whereas a writ under Art 226 must be moved by a party.

**Q6. Answer: (c)** - *Moderate* - Art 221 - salaries and allowances are charged on the State's Consolidated Fund; pensions are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India. Art 220 bars a retired permanent High Court judge from pleading in any court or before any authority in India EXCEPT the Supreme Court and the other High Courts. Statement 3 overstates the bar and is wrong.

**Q7. Answer: (d)** - *Hard* - Art 224A allows the Chief Justice of a High Court, with the previous consent of the President, to request a retired judge of that or any other High Court to sit and act. Such a judge enjoys all the jurisdiction, powers and privileges of a judge of that High Court, but is NOT otherwise deemed to be a judge of it. Statement 3 is therefore wrong.

**Q8. Answer: (b)** - *Moderate* - Art 231 (inserted by the 7th Amendment, 1956) empowers Parliament to establish a common High Court for two or more States, or for States and a Union Territory - Punjab and Haryana, and Bombay, are examples. All High Court judges, however, are appointed by the President under Art 217; the Governor is only one of the consultees. Statement 2 is wrong.

**Q9. Answer: (b)** - *Easy* - Art 233 - the Governor appoints, posts and promotes district judges in consultation with the High Court. Art 235 vests control over district courts and subordinate courts, including posting, promotion and leave of persons in the State judicial service below the rank of district judge, in the High Court. Both statements are correct.

**Q10. Answer: (d)** - *Moderate* - Art 312 permits Parliament to create new all-India services, including an all-India judicial service, but only after the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution supported by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting. The same article expressly provides that such a judicial service shall not include any post inferior to that of a district judge. Statement 3 is wrong.

**Q11. Answer: (a)** - *Hard* - All four are correct. Art 323A is confined to public service matters and is a Parliament-only power (CAT was set up under it in 1985); Art 323B covers an enumerated list - taxation, foreign exchange, industrial and labour disputes, land reforms, ceiling on urban property, elections to Parliament and State legislatures, food, rent and tenancy - and is available to Parliament and State legislatures alike. Part XIV-A came in with the 42nd Amendment, 1976. L. Chandra Kumar (1997) restored High Court review under Arts 226/227 and struck down the exclusion of that jurisdiction, making tribunals supplementary to, not substitutes for, the High Courts.

**Q12. Answer: (c)** - *Easy* - Art 324 vests superintendence, direction and control of these elections in the ECI (note: elections to panchayats and municipalities are handled by the State Election Commissions under Arts 243K and 243ZA). The Constitution leaves the number of Election Commissioners to the President - it fixes no number. The ECI was single-member from 1950, briefly three-member in Oct 1989 - Jan 1990, and has been multi-member continuously only since 1 October 1993. Statements 2 and 3 are wrong.

**Q13. Answer: (d)** - *Moderate* - The security of tenure is asymmetric: the CEC is removable only in the manner and on the grounds applicable to a Supreme Court judge, while other ECs (and Regional Commissioners) are removable by the President only on the CEC's recommendation. The Constitution prescribes no qualifications - legal, educational, administrative or judicial - for these offices, and no bar on post-retirement appointment. Statement 3 is wrong.

**Q14. Answer: (c)** - *Moderate* - All three are correctly matched. The 89th Amendment (2003) split the erstwhile joint commission and inserted Art 338A for the NCST. The 102nd Amendment (2018) inserted Art 338B, converting the NCBC from a statutory body under the NCBC Act, 1993 into a constitutional one. The 7th Amendment (1956), acting on the States Reorganisation Commission's advice, inserted Art 350B - note that this is a constitutional OFFICE (the Commissioner for Linguistic Minorities), not a commission, and the Constitution prescribes neither qualifications nor tenure for it.

**Q15. Answer: (a)** - *Easy* - Art 148 - appointment by warrant under the President's hand and seal; tenure of six years or age 65, whichever is earlier; removal in the same manner and on the same grounds as a Supreme Court judge. Crucially, after demitting office the CAG is INELIGIBLE for any further office under the Union or any State - a deliberate insulation against the prospect of a post-retirement reward. Statement 3 is wrong.

**Q16. Answer: (c)** - *Hard* - Only statement 2 is correct. Unlike the British Comptroller and Auditor General, India's CAG has the role of an auditor only, not of a comptroller: money can be drawn from the Consolidated Fund without his approval, and he audits expenditure AFTER it has been incurred. He is described as the 'friend, philosopher and guide' of the Public Accounts Committee, and he assists it - but he is not a member of it.

**Q17. Answer: (b)** - *Moderate* - Arts 315-323. The Constitution fixes neither the strength nor the qualifications of UPSC members - both are left to the President. Tenure is six years or age 65. But the UPSC Chairman is INELIGIBLE for any further employment under the Government of India or of a State, including reappointment as Chairman. A UPSC member, by contrast, may go on to become UPSC Chairman or the Chairman of a State PSC, and nothing else. Statement 3 is wrong.

**Q18. Answer: (c)** - *Moderate* - All three are correct, and the combination is the exam point: appointment is by the Governor, but removal is a presidential power alone - a State cannot dismiss its own PSC members. The retirement age is 62 for a State PSC (against 65 for the UPSC). Under Art 317, removal on the ground of misbehaviour requires a reference to, and an inquiry by, the Supreme Court, whose advice in this case is binding on the President.

**Q19. Answer: (d)** - *Moderate* - Art 280 - a quasi-judicial body constituted by the President every fifth year or earlier, with a Chairman and four other members whose qualifications and manner of selection Parliament prescribes (the Finance Commission (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1951). Its recommendations are ADVISORY only; they bind no one, and the Union has in practice accepted the core devolution recommendations by convention rather than by compulsion. The Sixteenth Finance Commission's award period runs from 2026-27 to 2030-31. Statement 3 is wrong.

**Q20. Answer: (c)** - *Moderate* - Art 279A was inserted by the 101st Amendment, 2016. The quorum is one-half of the total members, and decisions need three-fourths of the weighted votes of those present and voting, with the Centre's vote weighted at one-third and all States together at two-thirds - so neither side can act alone. In Union of India v. Mohit Minerals (2022) the Supreme Court held that the Council's recommendations are persuasive, not binding, since both Parliament and the State legislatures have simultaneous power to legislate on GST. Statement 3 is wrong.

**Q21. Answer: (d)** - *Hard* - Only statement 1 is correct. Under Art 88 the Attorney General has the right of audience in all courts, and the right to speak and take part in the proceedings of both Houses, any joint sitting, and any committee of which he is named a member - but NO right to vote. He is not a whole-time counsel of the Government and is not a member of the Cabinet; he is permitted private practice, subject to the bars on advising against the Government of India and on defending accused persons without the Government's permission. The Solicitor General and Additional Solicitors General assist him but find no mention in the Constitution.

**Q22. Answer: (b)** - *Easy* - PMKSY (Scheme for Agro-Marine Processing and Development of Agro-Processing Clusters) is an umbrella scheme of the Ministry of Food Processing Industries. Its components include Mega Food Parks, Integrated Cold Chain and Value Addition Infrastructure, Creation/Expansion of Food Processing and Preservation Capacities, Agro-Processing Clusters, Backward and Forward Linkages, Food Safety and Quality Assurance Infrastructure, and Operation Greens. Do not confuse the nodal ministry with the Ministry of Agriculture, which handles production rather than processing.

**Q23. Answer: (b)** - *Easy* - FSSAI is a statutory body created by the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and is headquartered in New Delhi. It works under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, not the Ministry of Food Processing Industries - a distinction UPSC has tested before, because food processing as an industry and food safety as a public-health function sit in different ministries. Statement 2 is wrong.

**Q24. Answer: (a)** - *Moderate* - All three are correctly matched. Operation Greens began with the 'TOP' crops - tomato, onion, potato - and was later expanded to a wider basket of notified fruits and vegetables ('TOP to TOTAL'). PLISFPI incentivises manufacture of identified food product categories and, distinctively, supports branding and marketing abroad. The Mega Food Park follows a cluster design - collection centres feed primary processing centres, which feed a central processing centre - as against an Agro-Processing Cluster, which is a smaller, demand-driven unit built around an existing production belt.

**Q25. Answer: (d)** - *Hard* - All three are correct. PMFME (launched 2020 under the Atmanirbhar Bharat package) is a centrally sponsored scheme of the Ministry of Food Processing Industries, with Centre-State cost sharing, that targets the unorganised micro segment. It offers a credit-linked capital subsidy to individual units, seed capital to SHG members, and grants to FPOs, producer cooperatives and SHGs, all organised around the One District One Product framework so that common infrastructure and branding can be shared within a district.

**Q26. Answer: (a)** - *Easy* - The services sector accounts for over half of India's Gross Value Added but employs a much smaller share of the workforce - roughly a third. This gap is the central puzzle of India's structural transformation: output moved out of agriculture much faster than labour did, so a large share of the workforce remains in low-productivity agriculture while the high-productivity services sector absorbs comparatively few workers.

**Q27. Answer: (d)** - *Moderate* - Mode 1 is cross-border supply; Mode 2 is consumption abroad (a foreign tourist or medical-value traveller consuming a service in India); Mode 3 is commercial presence (a subsidiary or branch); Mode 4 is the temporary presence of natural persons. Statement 3 describes Mode 3, not Mode 2, and is therefore wrong. India's offensive interest in services trade negotiations lies chiefly in Modes 1 and 4.

**Q28. Answer: (a)** - *Moderate* - PM GatiShakti (2021) is a digital, GIS-based National Master Plan that layers the infrastructure plans of the economic ministries onto a single map so that projects are planned and sequenced together instead of in silos. The National Logistics Policy (2022) is its soft-infrastructure complement, aimed at cutting logistics cost as a share of GDP and improving India's Logistics Performance Index position. Both are driven by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, not by MoRTH. Statement 3 is wrong.

**Q29. Answer: (a)** - *Hard* - NaBFID was set up under the National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development Act, 2021 as a development financial institution to provide long-term, non-recourse infrastructure finance and to deepen the domestic bond and derivatives markets. It is regulated and supervised by the RBI as an All India Financial Institution, alongside NABARD, SIDBI, EXIM Bank and NHB. It was established with government capital, so statement 3 is wrong.

**Q30. Answer: (d)** - *Easy* - Dadabhai Naoroji wrote Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901), the fullest statement of the drain theory; Romesh Chunder Dutt wrote The Economic History of India. Along with M.G. Ranade and G.V. Joshi, they built the Moderates' economic critique - the argument that British rule was draining India's wealth through Home Charges, interest on public debt, guaranteed railway returns and official remittances, an export surplus that bought India nothing in return.

**Q31. Answer: (d)** - *Moderate* - All three are correct. The Permanent Settlement (1793) was introduced by Cornwallis in Bengal, Bihar and Odisha, later extended to the Northern Circars and the Varanasi district. The Ryotwari system, associated with Thomas Munro and Alexander Read, settled revenue directly with the cultivating ryot in the Madras and Bombay Presidencies (and later Assam and Coorg). The Mahalwari system was framed by Holt Mackenzie in 1822 and revised under R.M. Bird in 1833, settling revenue with the village community or mahal in the North-Western Provinces, Punjab and parts of Central India.

**Q32. Answer: (a)** - *Moderate* - The zamindars were recognised as proprietors on condition of paying a revenue fixed in perpetuity, set at 10/11ths of the rental with 1/11th retained; the Sunset Law made punctuality absolute, and large numbers of old zamindaris changed hands at auction in the first two decades. It was never extended to the whole of British India - roughly nineteen per cent of British India came under it, while the Ryotwari and Mahalwari systems covered most of the rest. Statement 3 is wrong.

**Q33. Answer: (c)** - *Moderate* - All three are correct. The Vernacular Press Act, 1878 was passed under Lytton and was popularly called 'the gagging Act': it applied only to vernacular papers, allowed magistrates to demand a bond and security from printers and publishers, and provided no right of appeal to a court of law. Ripon repealed it in 1882. The Amrita Bazar Patrika famously converted overnight into an English language paper to escape it.

**Q34. Answer: (b)** - *Easy* - Charles Metcalfe, as acting Governor-General, repealed the restrictive Licensing Regulations of 1823 through the Press Act of 1835, earning the title 'liberator of the Indian press'. For contrast: Wellesley enacted the Censorship of Press Act, 1799 (pre-censorship of all newspapers); John Adam's Licensing Regulations of 1823 required a licence for every press; and Lytton passed the Vernacular Press Act, 1878.

**Q35. Answer: (b)** - *Moderate* - All three are correct. Wood's Despatch asked for a department of public instruction in each of the five provinces, universities on the London model at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras (established 1857), a graded system of schools, government support to a network of aided private schools, vernacular instruction at the primary level with English at higher levels, and attention to vocational and women's education. It set the architecture of Indian education for the rest of the colonial period.

**Q36. Answer: (a)** - *Hard* - Charter Act of 1813 (one lakh rupees a year for the revival of literature and the encouragement of the learned natives of India) - Hunter Commission, 1882 (primary and secondary education, appointed under Ripon) - Indian Universities Act, 1904 (following the Raleigh Commission, 1902, tightening government control over universities under Curzon) - Sadler Commission, 1917-19 (on Calcutta University, but reviewing the whole system). Correct order: 2-1-4-3. The Hartog Committee (1929) and the Sargent Plan (1944) come later still.

**Q37. Answer: (d)** - *Easy* - All three are correctly matched. Lothal, on the Bhogava in Gujarat, has the structure widely interpreted as a dockyard, along with rice husk and fire altars. Kalibangan, on the Ghaggar in Rajasthan, yielded a ploughed field from the pre-Harappan level and a row of fire altars. Dholavira, in the Rann of Kutch, is distinguished by its three-part town plan and its elaborate system of rock-cut water reservoirs, and by the large 'signboard' inscription.

**Q38. Answer: (d)** - *Moderate* - Chanhudaro, a bead-making and craft centre in Sindh, is the one major site excavated without a citadel. Surkotada in Gujarat produced the bone finds identified by some scholars as horse remains - a contested but frequently examined point. Rakhigarhi, however, is in Hisar district of HARYANA, not Gujarat, and is among the largest Harappan sites known. Statement 3 is wrong.

**Q39. Answer: (a)** - *Moderate* - The script, with roughly 375-400 signs, is written boustrophedon - right to left on the first line, left to right on the next - and has not been deciphered. Standardised chert weights follow the ratios 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 in the lower denominations and then proceed in decimal multiples of 16. What has NOT been found is any structure that can be identified with confidence as a temple or a palace - one of the civilisation's most striking silences and a favourite Prelims point. Statement 3 is wrong.

**Q40. Answer: (c)** - *Easy* - Mesopotamian texts refer to trade with Dilmun (generally identified with Bahrain), Magan (Oman) and Meluhha, the last of which is usually taken to be the Harappan region. Harappan seals found at Mesopotamian sites, and finds of carnelian beads, shell and timber, corroborate the link.

**Q41. Answer: (a)** - *Moderate* - The dasarajna, in which the Bharata chief Sudas defeated a confederacy of ten tribes, was fought on the Parushni (the modern Ravi). The Sabha, Samiti, Vidatha and Gana are the assemblies named in the Rig Veda. But the fourfold varna order appears only in the Purusha Sukta of the tenth mandala, generally regarded as a late addition; through the rest of the text social divisions are fluid and occupational rather than hereditary and rigid. Statement 3 is wrong.

**Q42. Answer: (c)** - *Hard* - All three are correct, and together they describe a single transition. The move east into the Ganga-Yamuna doab is accompanied by Painted Grey Ware and the growing use of iron, by a shift from a largely pastoral to a settled agrarian economy, by the enlargement of the jana into the janapada and of the rajan into a samrat, and by the elaboration of great royal sacrifices - rajasuya (consecration), ashvamedha (horse sacrifice asserting supremacy) and vajapeya (a chariot race conferring pre-eminence) - which is precisely how ritual came to do the work of legitimising the new territorial kingship.

**Q43. Answer: (c)** - *Easy* - Rural settlements in India are classified as clustered (nucleated), semi-clustered or fragmented, hamleted, and dispersed or isolated. A conurbation is an urban form - a large area formed by the merging of several towns and cities into a continuous built-up mass (the term is Patrick Geddes's) - and is therefore not a rural settlement type.

**Q44. Answer: (a)** - *Moderate* - All three conditions must be satisfied together for a census town. Note the contrast with a STATUTORY town, which is any place with a municipality, corporation, cantonment board or notified town area committee, regardless of these three criteria. The distinction matters because much of the growth in India's recorded urban population comes from new census towns rather than from the expansion of statutory ones.

**Q45. Answer: (b)** - *Easy* - All three are correct. Kharif is the monsoon crop - rice, jowar, bajra, maize, cotton, groundnut, jute. Rabi is the winter crop, dependent on winter precipitation and irrigation - wheat, barley, gram, mustard, peas. Zaid is the short summer season between the two, when watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, fodder crops and some vegetables are grown on irrigated land.

**Q46. Answer: (a)** - *Moderate* - Culturable waste is land available for cultivation but left uncultivated for more than five agricultural years in a row; current fallow is left uncultivated for one agricultural year, and fallow other than current fallow for one to five years. Gross cropped area, however, is the net sown area PLUS the area sown more than once in an agricultural year - fallow land is by definition not sown, so it cannot be added in. Statement 3 is wrong.

**Q47. Answer: (c)** - *Easy* - All three are correct. CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) with the Cas9 endonuclease is derived from a bacterial defence system that stores fragments of invading viral DNA and uses them to recognise the invader on its return. In the engineered version, a synthetic guide RNA carries Cas9 to a chosen sequence, where it makes a double-strand break; the cell's own repair machinery then produces the edit. Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna received the 2020 Chemistry Nobel for it.

**Q48. Answer: (b)** - *Moderate* - Bt cotton remains the only GM crop cleared for commercial cultivation; Bt brinjal was placed under an indefinite moratorium in 2010 and GM mustard DMH-11 remains in litigation. The Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee is the apex approval body under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, operating under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and the Rules of 1989 - not under the Department of Biotechnology, so statement 2 is wrong. In March 2022 the Ministry exempted SDN-1 and SDN-2 genome-edited plants free of exogenous DNA from Rules 7 to 11 of the 1989 Rules; SDN-3, which introduces foreign DNA, continues to be regulated as a GMO.

**Q49. Answer: (c)** - *Hard* - Covaxin uses a whole inactivated virion with an adjuvant; Covishield is a replication-deficient chimpanzee adenovirus vector carrying the spike protein gene. CERVAVAC is India's first indigenously developed quadrivalent vaccine against the human papillomavirus, aimed at cervical cancer - not tuberculosis - so statement 3 is wrong. Note also ZyCoV-D, the world's first approved plasmid DNA vaccine for human use.

**Q50. Answer: (c)** - *Moderate* - All three are correct. The Declaration on Strategic Partnership was signed in October 2000 and institutionalised an annual summit; the partnership was upgraded to a 'Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership' in 2010. BrahMos Aerospace is an India-Russia joint venture producing the supersonic cruise missile, and is now an export platform in its own right. The other pillars to hold: defence (S-400, the AK-203 project at Korwa, licensed production), energy (crude imports, Sakhalin and other equity stakes, Kudankulam), and connectivity (the International North-South Transport Corridor, the Chennai-Vladivostok Eastern Maritime Corridor).


## Revision checklist (drill these cold)

1. **High Court articles:** 214 (a HC per State) · 215 (court of record) · **216 - no maximum strength prescribed** · 217 (10 yrs judicial office OR 10 yrs advocate; **no distinguished-jurist route**; retires at **62**) · 221 (salaries on **State** CF, pensions on **Union** CF) · 222 transfer · **224A** retired judge, previous consent of the **President**, but **not deemed a judge for all purposes** · 226 writs · 227 superintendence · 228 transfer of cases · 231 common HC by **Parliament**.
2. **226 vs 32, cold:** 226 is **wider** (rights *and any other purpose*), is a **constitutional right, not a Fundamental Right**, is **discretionary** (can be refused), and reaches authorities outside the territory where the **cause of action** arises (**15th Amendment, 1963**). Art 32 is narrower, is itself a Fundamental Right, cannot be refused.
3. **Art 227** covers all courts and tribunals in the State **except military courts/tribunals**; it is judicial *and* administrative, and can be exercised **suo motu**.
4. **Subordinate judiciary:** Arts 233-237. **Governor appoints** district judges in consultation with the HC; **control vests in the High Court** (Art 235). **AIJS under Art 312** needs a **Rajya Sabha resolution by 2/3rds present and voting** and **cannot include a post below district judge**.
5. **Tribunals:** **323A** = public service matters, **Parliament only** (CAT, 1985); **323B** = enumerated list, **Parliament or State legislatures**; Part XIV-A inserted by the **42nd Amendment, 1976**; ***L. Chandra Kumar* (1997)** kept HC review under 226/227 alive - tribunals supplement, never substitute, the High Courts.
6. **ECI:** Art 324; **multi-member only since 1 Oct 1993**; Constitution prescribes **no number, no qualifications, no bar on post-retirement office**. **CEC removable like an SC judge; other ECs only on the CEC's recommendation.** CEC and Other ECs Act, **2023**.
7. **CAG:** Arts 148-151; warrant under hand and seal; **6 yrs or 65**; **ineligible for any further office** thereafter; **auditor, not comptroller** - no control over issue of money from the CFI, audits *after* expenditure; **"friend, philosopher and guide" to the PAC but not a member of it**.
8. **The tenure table:** UPSC **6 yrs / 65** · State PSC **6 yrs / 62** · CAG **6 yrs / 65** · CEC & ECs **6 yrs / 65**. **State PSC members are appointed by the Governor but removable only by the President**, on an **Art 317** Supreme Court inquiry whose advice is **binding**.
9. **Post-tenure bars:** UPSC Chairman - **nothing further, not even reappointment**; UPSC member - may become **UPSC Chairman or a State PSC Chairman only**; CAG - **nothing at all**; CEC - **no bar in the Constitution**.
10. **Advisory, not binding:** **Finance Commission** (Art 280, every fifth year or earlier, qualifications set by **Parliament**, **16th FC award period 2026-27 to 2030-31**) · **UPSC advice** (non-acceptance memorandum laid before Parliament) · **GST Council** (Art 279A, 101st Amendment 2016, quorum 50%, **3/4ths weighted votes, Centre 1/3 + States 2/3**; ***Mohit Minerals* 2022** - persuasive only).
11. **Commissions and their amendments:** **338 NCSC** · **338A NCST (89th, 2003)** · **338B NCBC (102nd, 2018; 105th, 2021 restored State power to identify SEBCs)** · **350B Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities (7th, 1956)** - an **office, not a commission**, with no prescribed qualifications or tenure. **Attorney General (Art 76):** SC-judge qualification, **right to speak in both Houses but no vote (Art 88)**, **not a Cabinet member, not a whole-time counsel, private practice permitted**; SG and ASGs are **not in the Constitution**.
12. **Food processing:** **PMKSY under MoFPI** (Mega Food Parks, cold chain, APCs, backward-forward linkages, **Operation Greens TOP -> TOTAL**) · **PMFME** = centrally sponsored, **ODOP**, credit-linked capital subsidy + SHG seed capital · **PLISFPI** uniquely funds **branding and marketing abroad** · **FSSAI is statutory under the FSS Act 2006 but sits under the Ministry of Health**.
13. **Services and infrastructure:** GVA share **>> employment share** - the structural-transformation gap. **GATS: Mode 1 cross-border, Mode 2 consumption abroad, Mode 3 commercial presence, Mode 4 natural persons**; India's interest is **1 and 4**. Services surplus offsets the merchandise deficit in the current account. **PM GatiShakti (2021) and NLP (2022) both under DPIIT**; **NaBFID (Act of 2021), RBI-regulated as an AIFI**.
14. **Land revenue, one table:** **Permanent Settlement 1793, Cornwallis, Bengal-Bihar-Odisha, 10/11ths to the state, Sunset Law, ~19% of British India** · **Ryotwari, Munro and Read, Madras-Bombay, settlement with the ryot, periodic revision** · **Mahalwari, Holt Mackenzie 1822 / R.M. Bird 1833, NWP-Punjab, settlement with the *mahal*, joint responsibility**. Drain: **Naoroji, *Poverty and Un-British Rule in India* (1901)**; **R.C. Dutt, *The Economic History of India***. **TISCO 1907.**
15. **Press ladder:** **1799 Censorship Act (Wellesley)** -> **1823 Licensing Regulations (John Adam)** -> **1835 Press Act (Metcalfe, "liberator of the press")** -> **1867 Registration Act** -> **1878 Vernacular Press Act (Lytton, repealed by Ripon 1882)** -> **1908 Newspapers (Incitement to Offences) Act** -> **1910 Indian Press Act**. **Education ladder:** **1813 Charter Act (Rs 1 lakh)** -> **1835 Macaulay's Minute** -> **1854 Wood's Despatch (Magna Carta)** -> **1882 Hunter** -> **1902 Raleigh / 1904 Indian Universities Act** -> **1917-19 Sadler** -> **1929 Hartog** -> **1944 Sargent**.
16. **Indus:** Lothal dockyard · Kalibangan ploughed field · Dholavira reservoirs and signboard · **Chanhudaro - the one major site with no citadel** · Surkotada horse bones · **Rakhigarhi is in Haryana, not Gujarat** · script **boustrophedon, undeciphered** · weights **binary below, decimal above 16** · **no definitively identified temple or palace** · **Meluhha** (Dilmun = Bahrain, Magan = Oman).
17. **Vedic:** **dasarajna on the Parushni (Ravi)**; Sabha, Samiti, Vidatha, Gana; **varna appears fully formed only in the late Purusha Sukta (10th mandala)**; Later Vedic = **eastward to the Ganga-Yamuna doab + PGW + iron + jana to janapada + rajasuya / ashvamedha / vajapeya**.
18. **Geography:** rural settlements = clustered / semi-clustered / hamleted / dispersed (**conurbation is urban**); **census town = 5,000 population AND 75% male non-agricultural workers AND 400 persons/km2 - all three**, whereas a **statutory town needs only a municipal body**; **gross cropped area = net sown area + area sown more than once** (not fallow); culturable waste = uncultivated **> 5 years**, current fallow = **1 year**.
19. **Biotech:** CRISPR-Cas9 from a **bacterial adaptive immune system**, guide RNA + Cas9 double-strand break, **2020 Chemistry Nobel (Charpentier and Doudna)**; **GEAC under MoEFCC**, EPA 1986 + Rules 1989; **Bt cotton is the only commercially cultivated GM crop**, Bt brinjal moratorium 2010, GM mustard DMH-11 in litigation; **SDN-1 and SDN-2 exempted (March 2022), SDN-3 still regulated**; **CERVAVAC = HPV**, Covaxin = inactivated, Covishield = viral vector, ZyCoV-D = DNA plasmid; **BioE3 Policy (Biotechnology for Economy, Environment and Employment), Cabinet approval Aug 2024**; Biological Diversity Act 2002 (amended 2023), NBA, Nagoya Protocol and ABS.
20. **India-Russia:** **Declaration on Strategic Partnership 2000** -> **Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership 2010**; annual summit + **IRIGC-TEC**; BrahMos JV, S-400, AK-203 at Korwa; Sakhalin, Kudankulam; **INSTC** and the **Chennai-Vladivostok Eastern Maritime Corridor**.
